unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 6! In this unit the focus is on people and work. You will explore the many different jobs and professions that keep communities running, from physicians and lawyers to food vendors and commentators. You will learn how people choose their careers, what skills different jobs require, and how the world of work connects to ideas of fairness, justice, and community responsibility.
unit.learningPath: Preview the goals and vocabulary. Read and annotate the source texts. Discuss evidence and language choices. Apply the grammar focus. Draft and revise two to three paragraphs. Present, reflect and complete the quiz.

visual.alt: Learners exploring careers, justice and community responsibility

readings.title: The People Who Keep a Community Running
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Every morning in the East African city of Hargeisa, hundreds of people set off to work. Some carry briefcases, some carry toolboxes, and some carry nothing but their knowledge and determination. Each person has a profession, a role that helps keep the community running smoothly. Understanding these roles can help you start thinking about your own future career.
Look closely and you will see how the professions fit together. The physician who opens the clinic at seven o'clock depends on the pharmacist next door and on the driver who brings medicines from the port. The teacher who unlocks the classroom depends on the carpenter who repaired the desks and on the food vendor who sells breakfast at the gate. No profession stands alone; each one is a link in a chain that reaches across the whole town.
Every profession asks for its own mixture of skills. Some, like a lawyer or a physician, need years of study and difficult examinations. Others, like a mechanic or a tailor, are learned with the hands, one repair or one seam at a time, often beside an older worker who passes on the craft. A radio commentator needs a clear voice and quick thinking; a shopkeeper needs patience and a head for figures. What all of them share is responsibility: people rely on them to do their work well and fairly.
Choosing a career starts with noticing what you enjoy and what you are good at. Do you like solving problems, or explaining things, or making something with your hands? Do you prefer working alone or in a busy team? Your interests and strengths are clues, and the working people around you every morning are the best examples of where those clues can lead.

readings.title: Four Professions, One Town
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
At the local hospital, a physician named Doctor Sarah begins her shift at seven o’clock. Her profession requires years of study. She completed medical school, passed difficult exams, and paid tuition fees that her family saved for over many years. Now she treats patients, reads test results, and gives careful observation reports to her team. Being a physician demands patience, scientific knowledge, and the ability to communicate clearly with people who are worried or in pain. Doctor Sarah always says that the most important quality in medicine is the wisdom to listen before you speak.
Across the road from the hospital, a young woman named Amara works as a legal advisor at a small law office. Her job involves studying legal documents, understanding the country’s laws, and giving people advice about their rights. She helps families settle disputes, assists business owners with contracts, and sometimes appears in courtrooms to defend her clients. Amara knows that legal penalties can be serious, so she works carefully and pays attention to every detail. She often reminds her younger siblings that a career in law requires strong reading skills, clear thinking, and a deep sense of fairness.
Not far away, in the busy Waheen market, a food vendor named Omar runs a popular stall. He has been selling freshly made sambusas and canjeero for over twenty years. Although he did not attend a university, Omar is one of the most efficient workers in the market. He wakes before dawn to prepare his ingredients, keeps his cooking area spotlessly clean to avoid any contaminated food, and manages his money carefully. His business skills are the result of decades of experience and wisdom passed down through his family. Omar proves that a valuable profession does not always require a formal qualification but always requires dedication and hard work.
At the local radio station, a commentator named Tariq records his evening programme. He writes a script for each broadcast, choosing his words carefully so that listeners can understand the day’s events. He reads figures and facts aloud, adds his own commentary, and invites guests to share their views. A commentator must be well-informed, confident, and able to explain complicated ideas in simple language. Tariq also writes captions for the station’s social media pages, making sure every post is accurate and clear.
These four people have very different jobs, yet they all share important qualities: responsibility, dedication, and a desire to serve their community. Whether you dream of becoming a historian, an inventor, a teacher, or something entirely different, the key is to discover what you love, develop the skills you need, and never stop learning. Your profession is not just what you do for money — it is how you contribute to the world around you.

readings.title: Voices in the Courtroom, part 1
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
The day of the trial felt different from every other in the town of Luyanda.
Shops opened more slowly. Motorbikes moved more quietly. Even the sky, usually so loud with birds, felt still.
Twelve-year-old Amal waited outside the school gate, clutching a folder full of papers. Her class was going on a field trip — not to the museum, or the zoo, but to the courtroom.
“We are currently observing a real case,” their teacher had said. “You’ll learn how rights, laws, and profession roles work in society.”
Amal had never stepped foot in a courthouse before. But she knew this was not a normal case.
It involved her neighbour, Mama Dina.
Mama Dina was a local food vendor who often gave Amal extra cassava or banana when she passed by. She was kind, wise, and popular. But last month, officials came to her stall and accused her of selling contaminated food.
They said her cooking water was unsafe. She was arrested, fined, and told she could no longer sell.
“I refuse to believe she did anything wrong,” Amal had told her parents.
“They say the test showed bacteria,” her mother had replied.
“She said the officer didn’t have her consent to test her pots,” Amal insisted.
“She told us,” her father added, “that the food wasn’t even served that day.”
Amal had listened to every word — and written it down. Now she carried those notes in her folder like evidence.
Inside the courthouse, rows of benches lined the walls. The room was full of murmurs. A judge in a black robe sat at the front. A commentator from the local radio station recorded notes for a short evening script.
The teacher handed out a sheet.
“Today, you will identify: the defence and prosecution; any compound nouns (such as tuition fees and legal penalties); verbs in present continuous; and new profession titles based on suffixes.”
Amal’s eyes danced across the list.
“The State v. Dina Okoro,” the bailiff announced.
A young physician testified first. “The test showed bacteria in the container,” he said. “Food from this water could cause illness.”
“But was food served that day?” asked the defence lawyer.
The physician hesitated. “We’re not currently sure.”
Amal scribbled: “Observation unclear. Present continuous used.”
Mama Dina’s commentary came next. She stood tall, her voice calm.
“The officer entered without asking. I never gave my consent. He touched my pots with gloves still dirty from the last stall. I told him: ‘That’s not allowed.’ But he wrote down his criticism anyway.”
Her lawyer nodded. “That’s reported speech. He said, she said.”

readings.title: Voices in the Courtroom, part 2
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
The teacher leaned over to Amal. “You’re doing good observation,” she whispered.
The prosecution argued that penalties must be applied equally. “All vendors must be inspected. Legal standards are there for a reason.”
“But,” Mama Dina’s lawyer said, “the process was flawed. If the action was unfair, the penalty is unconstitutional.”
Amal whispered to her classmate: “That means it goes against the rules of the country.”
The judge listened quietly, taking notes with a blue pen. His face revealed nothing.
After a break, the students gathered under a tree beside the courthouse.
“I still don’t understand,” one boy said. “If there were figures, like test results, doesn’t that mean she’s guilty?”
“But the figures might be wrong,” Amal argued. “And even good data needs good methods.”
“It’s like when you study heredity in science,” said a girl. “You can’t just assume something based on one test.”
Their teacher nodded. “Good thinking. Scientific wisdom applies in court too. Look at all sides.”
Back inside, a final witness spoke: a food safety commentator from the city.
“She is efficient, yes,” the woman said. “But during food checks, many women vendors are targeted more. We need more fair integration, not more bias or segregation.”
“Please avoid political speech,” said the prosecution.
But the judge replied, “Injustice is always political. Proceed.”
The trial ended, and the judge said he would return a verdict the next day.
As the students filed out, the teacher asked them to write a reflection.
“Today we saw how laws are made and used. But rules must be fair. When someone like Mama Dina is punished unfairly, people lose trust. Good observation is like science. It takes patience and care. I want to be a commentator, a legal advisor, or maybe a historian one day — someone who helps stories stay true.”
That night, Amal told her parents everything.
“She said the officer never washed his gloves. She said she never served that day.”
“She said the criticism was false,” her father added.
Her mother nodded. “She said the penalty wasn’t fair.”
“Exactly!” Amal smiled. “We all used reported speech. We all noticed the same things.”
The next morning, the town was waiting.
The judge read aloud: “The evidence was incomplete. The officer’s observation lacked protocol. The penalty is dropped. Mama Dina is free to return to her profession.”
Amal did not jump or cheer. She just grinned, wide and quiet.
The woman touched her shoulder. “Thank you. Your presence mattered.”
Amal felt her heart fill. It was a small moment — but powerful.
The next week, the students wrote scripts of the event for a class radio play. Amal helped add captions under printed photos, and even wrote the commentary for the narrator.

comprehension.explanation: The second paragraph gives the chain image and two worked examples: the clinic depends on the pharmacy and the medicine driver, and the school depends on the carpenter and the food vendor.

comprehension.question: The writer describes four very different jobs. What qualities does the passage say they share, and why does it end with advice to the reader?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The passage says all four share responsibility, dedication and a desire to serve their community, and it ends with advice to encourage the reader to find work they love.
comprehension.explanation: The final paragraph lists the shared qualities and then advises the reader to discover what they love and keep learning, which gives the text an encouraging tone.

comprehension.question: How does the writer create a quiet, tense mood at the very start of part one? Refer to details from the text.
comprehension.correctAnswer: The writer says the shops opened more slowly, the motorbikes moved more quietly, and even the usually noisy sky felt still, which builds a tense, waiting mood.
comprehension.explanation: The opening lines describe slow shops, quieter motorbikes and a still sky to signal that this day of the trial feels different and tense.

comprehension.question: In her reflection, Amal compares good observation to science. Explain what she means and how it connects to the trial's outcome.
comprehension.correctAnswer: She means good observation, like science, needs patience, care and reliable methods; because the officer's method lacked protocol, the evidence could not be trusted and the penalty was dropped.
comprehension.explanation: Amal writes that good observation is like science and takes patience and care, and the verdict agrees, dropping the penalty because the officer's observation lacked protocol.

grammar.title: Compound Nouns: Closed, Hyphenated and Open Forms
grammar.explanation: A compound noun joins two or more words to make one noun with a single, specific meaning, and English writes these compounds in three different forms.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: A compound noun combines words so the first word usually tells you what kind of the second: tuition tells you what kind of fees. There are three forms. Closed form is one word: toothbrush, football, classroom, courtroom, headmaster, newspaper. Hyphenated form is joined by a hyphen: mother-in-law, well-being, check-up, passer-by, six-year-old. Open form is two separate words that act as one: tuition fees, legal penalties, bus stop, swimming pool, police officer, food vendor, test results. A swimming pool is a special kind of pool, not a pool that is swimming.
grammar.commonMistake: Mistake: writing an open compound as one word, such as 'swimmingpool', or hyphenating it as 'swimming-pool'. Fix: check a dictionary, because 'swimming pool' is open, 'toothbrush' is closed and 'check-up' is hyphenated.
grammar.memoryTip: Ask whether the two words together mean something new; if they do, you have a compound noun, and then you decide closed, hyphenated or open.
grammar.practice:
Part A: sort these into closed, hyphenated or open form — toothbrush, bus stop, mother-in-law, classroom, swimming pool, check-up, football, police officer, well-being, tuition fees. Part B: write one clear sentence about work for a closed, a hyphenated and an open compound noun.

ANSWER KEY (self-check - complete Parts A and B first, then check your work):
Part A: Closed - toothbrush, classroom, football. Hyphenated - mother-in-law, check-up, well-being. Open - bus stop, swimming pool, police officer, tuition fees.
Part B (model example - this is open-ended, so your own sentences are correct if the compound noun form matches): Closed: 'The headmaster gave a speech in the classroom.' Hyphenated: 'After his check-up, the worker felt a new sense of well-being.' Open: 'The police officer checked the test results before the job interview.'

grammar.title: Building Compound Nouns for the World of Work
grammar.explanation: Compound nouns follow predictable patterns, and the world of work is full of them, so learning the patterns helps you name working ideas precisely.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Common patterns build compound nouns: noun plus noun (courtroom, bus stop), adjective plus noun (greenhouse, high court), verb plus noun (swimming pool, washing machine), noun plus verb (sunrise, haircut) and verb plus preposition (check-up, workout). Work examples include job interview, business owner, fire station, police officer, food vendor, test results, script writing, health worker and radio presenter. To build one, put the describing word first, because script writing means the writing of scripts, and then check the correct form.
grammar.commonMistake: Mistake: reversing the order, such as 'fees tuition' instead of 'tuition fees'. Fix: put the describing word first, because the first word tells you what kind of the second.
grammar.memoryTip: Describer first, thing second: 'fire' plus 'station' names the station for fires.
grammar.practice:
Part A: match a word from each list to make a compound noun and write a sentence for each — fire and station, head and master, script and writing, legal and penalties, ice and cream. Part B: complete each gap in your book using courtroom, tuition fees, test results, food vendor, migration path and check-up.

ANSWER KEY (self-check - complete Parts A and B first, then check your work):
Part A matches: fire + station = fire station; head + master = headmaster; script + writing = script writing; legal + penalties = legal penalties; ice + cream = ice cream. (Model sentences - open-ended, your own is correct if it uses the compound noun correctly): 'The fire station sent two lorries to help.' 'The headmaster welcomed the new students.' 'Script writing takes patience and careful editing.' 'The legal penalties for the crime were severe.' 'She bought ice cream after her interview.'
Part B (the exact gapped sentences are in your workbook, not reproduced here, so use this meaning check instead of a fixed answer): courtroom = the room where a trial is held; tuition fees = money paid for schooling or lessons; test results = the outcome of a test; food vendor = a person who sells food; migration path = the route people or animals migrate along; check-up = a routine examination. Confirm the word you chose matches the meaning needed in each gap.

grammar.title: Reported Speech: Shifting Tense and Pronouns
grammar.explanation: Reported speech retells what someone said without their exact words, so you remove the quotation marks and usually shift the tense back one step and change the pronouns.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Direct speech uses quotation marks, but reported speech does not. Shift the tense back one step: present simple to past simple (I work becomes she said she worked), present continuous to past continuous (I am writing becomes she said she was writing), past simple to past perfect (I finished becomes he said he had finished), will to would and can to could. Change the pronouns to match the reporter. Direct: 'I love my job,' said the doctor. Reported: The doctor said that she loved her job. The word that is optional.
grammar.commonMistake: Mistake: keeping the present tense, such as 'She said that she works at the hospital'. Fix: shift it back to 'She said that she worked at the hospital'.
grammar.memoryTip: Step one tense back in time, and turn the pronouns to fit the person now telling the story.
grammar.practice:
Part A: rewrite in reported speech — 'I need the test results,' said the doctor; 'I am studying the documents,' said the advisor; 'I will write the script tomorrow,' said the presenter. Part B: explain the tense change you made in each sentence.

ANSWER KEY (self-check - complete Parts A and B first, then check your work):
Part A: 'I need the test results,' said the doctor -> The doctor said that they needed the test results. 'I am studying the documents,' said the advisor -> The advisor said that they were studying the documents. 'I will write the script tomorrow,' said the presenter -> The presenter said that they would write the script the next day (you will learn why 'tomorrow' becomes 'the next day' in the next lesson).
Part B: 1) present simple 'need' shifts to past simple 'needed', and 'I' shifts to 'they'. 2) present continuous 'am studying' shifts to past continuous 'were studying', and 'I' shifts to 'they'. 3) 'will write' shifts to 'would write', and 'I' shifts to 'they'.

grammar.title: Reported Speech: Time Words, Said and Told
grammar.explanation: When you report speech, some time and place words change, and you choose between said and told depending on whether you name the listener.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Time and place words shift in reported speech: today becomes that day, tomorrow becomes the next day, yesterday becomes the day before, now becomes then, here becomes there and this becomes that. Use said when you do not name the listener (He said that he was tired) and told when you do name the listener (He told me that he was tired). Direct: 'I will finish it today,' she said. Reported: She said that she would finish it that day.
grammar.commonMistake: Mistake: writing 'He told that he was busy', with no listener after told. Fix: name the listener with 'He told me that he was busy', or use said instead.
grammar.memoryTip: Told needs a person straight after it, but said does not; and today slides to that day.
grammar.practice:
Part A: report these and change the time words — 'We are visiting the courthouse today,' said the teacher; 'I finished the report yesterday,' said the clerk. Part B: rewrite each sentence once with said and once with told, adding a listener.

ANSWER KEY (self-check - complete Parts A and B first, then check your work):
Part A: 'We are visiting the courthouse today,' said the teacher -> The teacher said that they were visiting the courthouse that day (are visiting -> were visiting; today -> that day). 'I finished the report yesterday,' said the clerk -> The clerk said that they had finished the report the day before (finished -> had finished; yesterday -> the day before).
Part B (model example - who you name as the listener is open-ended, so your own name or job title is correct as long as said/told are used correctly): Sentence 1 - Said: 'The teacher said that they were visiting the courthouse that day.' Told: 'The teacher told the class that they were visiting the courthouse that day.' Sentence 2 - Said: 'The clerk said that they had finished the report the day before.' Told: 'The clerk told the manager that they had finished the report the day before.'

grammar.title: Reporting Questions and Commands
grammar.explanation: Questions and commands change shape in reported speech, because questions become statements and commands use told plus a person plus to.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Report a question with statement word order and no question mark. Direct: 'Where do you work?' Reported: She asked where I worked. For a yes or no question, use if or whether. Direct: 'Do you like your job?' Reported: She asked if I liked my job. Report a command with told plus a person plus to plus the base verb. Direct: 'Close the door.' Reported: She told him to close the door. For a negative command, add not: She told him not to open the window.
grammar.commonMistake: Mistake: keeping question word order, such as 'She asked where did I work'. Fix: use statement order, 'She asked where I worked', with no did and no question mark.
grammar.memoryTip: A reported question stops asking and starts telling: question word, then a plain statement.
grammar.practice:
Part A: report these questions — 'What is a compound noun?' asked the student; 'Did the officer have consent?' asked the lawyer. Part B: report two commands using told plus a person plus to, and make one of them a negative command.

ANSWER KEY (self-check - complete Parts A and B first, then check your work):
Part A: 'What is a compound noun?' asked the student -> The student asked what a compound noun was (is -> was; statement word order, no question mark). 'Did the officer have consent?' asked the lawyer -> The lawyer asked whether the officer had had consent (did have -> had had; statement word order) - this echoes the courtroom reading where Mama Dina says the officer did not have her consent.
Part B (model example - this is open-ended, so your own two commands are correct if they follow the told + person + to pattern): Affirmative - Direct: 'Close the door.' Reported: 'She told him to close the door.' Negative - Direct: 'Don't open the window.' Reported: 'She told him not to open the window.'

grammar.title: Present Continuous for the Future and Profession Suffixes
grammar.explanation: The present continuous can describe fixed future arrangements, and profession suffixes turn base words into job titles, so both are useful when you write about work.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Use the present continuous for a planned future arrangement with a time reference: She is starting her new job on Monday. The manager is meeting the team tomorrow. Profession suffixes build job titles: -ian gives physician, historian and librarian; -or gives commentator, inspector and director; -er gives teacher, presenter and manager; and -ist gives scientist, journalist and artist. Add the suffix to a base, so history plus -ian makes historian and science plus -ist makes scientist.
grammar.commonMistake: Mistake: choosing the wrong suffix, such as 'historier' or 'scienter'. Fix: learn the correct ending, historian and scientist, by reading widely and checking a dictionary.
grammar.memoryTip: For a planned future, use be plus verb-ing plus a time, as in 'is starting on Monday'; for jobs, try -ian, -or, -er and -ist.
grammar.practice:
Part A: write three sentences about planned future events at work using the present continuous and a time word. Part B: build a job title from each base with a suffix — history, science, comment and teach — then use two of them in sentences.

ANSWER KEY (self-check - complete Parts A and B first, then check your work):
Part A (model example - this is open-ended, so your own three sentences are correct if they use present continuous plus a time word for a planned future event): 'She is starting her new job on Monday.' 'The manager is meeting the team tomorrow.' 'He is presenting his report next week.'
Part B: history + -ian = historian; science + -ist = scientist; comment + -or = commentator; teach + -er = teacher. (Model sentences for two of them - open-ended, your own is correct if the title is used properly): 'The historian explained the old trial records.' 'The scientist studied the test results carefully.'

speaking.title: Speaking 1: Career Interview Role-Play
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines: In this activity, one person plays the role of a worker and the other plays the role of a journalist. The journalist interviews the worker about their profession. Here is how to play. First, the worker chooses a profession, either one from this unit or any other job they know about. Second, the journalist prepares at least five questions to ask, such as: What does your job involve? What skills do you need? What is the most challenging part of your work? What advice would you give to a young person who wants to do this job? Third, the journalist asks the questions and listens carefully to the answers. Fourth, after the interview, the journalist reports what the worker said using reported speech. For example: She told me that her job involved reading legal documents. He said that the most challenging part was working long hours. Swap roles and play again with a different profession.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Help me practise career interview role-play and give feedback on clarity, vocabulary and complete sentences.

Play at least five rounds with a different job each time, and after each round say one compound noun that is linked to the job.

writing.title: Writing 1: Job Advertisement
writing.promptAndInstructions: Imagine you are the manager of a business and you need to hire a new worker. Write a job advertisement of about 150 to 200 words that describes the role and encourages the right person to apply. Include a clear job title (use a compound noun such as project manager, food inspector or radio presenter), a short description of the organisation, a list of daily responsibilities, a list of requirements, information about salary or working hours, and a final persuasive sentence that encourages people to apply.
writing.modelText:
Wanted: Food Inspector for Hargeisa City Council.
We are a small, efficient team that keeps the markets of Hargeisa safe. Every day you will visit food vendors, take samples, write observation reports and explain the legal rules politely.
You need a science certificate, two years of experience and the wisdom to listen before you speak. The salary is 900 dollars a month, Monday to Friday, eight until four.
If you care about clean food and a healthy community, apply today.

items: Job title line: Wanted: Radio Presenter for Radio Berbera.

Paragraph 1 (organisation and daily responsibilities): We are a small, friendly team that broadcasts news and music to the whole town. Every day you will prepare a playlist, interview local guests, read the news bulletin and answer calls from listeners live on air.

Paragraph 2 (requirements and salary or hours): You need a clear speaking voice, basic computer skills and the confidence to think quickly during a live broadcast. The salary is 700 dollars a month, Tuesday to Saturday, two until eight in the evening.
Paragraph 3 (persuasive closing sentence): If you love talking to people and sharing good news, apply today.

writing.title: Writing 2: Career Presentation
writing.promptAndInstructions: Choose a profession that interests you, such as a doctor, teacher, engineer, artist, farmer or journalist. Write a career presentation of about 150 to 200 words that you could give to your class. Introduce the profession and say why you chose it, describe what a person in this job does each day, explain the skills and qualifications it needs, use at least one compound noun and one sentence of reported speech, and finish by explaining how the profession helps the community.
writing.modelText:
I would like to explain why I want to be a physician. I chose this profession after I met Doctor Sarah at the hospital in Hargeisa.
Every day she treats patients, reads test results and writes observation reports for her team. It needs years of study, expensive tuition fees and a lot of patience. She told me that the most important quality in medicine was the wisdom to listen.
A physician helps the whole community, because when people are healthy they can work, learn and look after their families.

items: Paragraph 1 (intro and why chosen): I would like to explain why I want to be a civil engineer. I chose this profession after I watched engineers repair the bridge near our neighbourhood.

Paragraph 2 (daily duties, skills, reported speech): Every day an engineer studies drawings, checks measurements and tests whether materials are strong enough. It needs years of study, careful mathematics and steady patience under pressure. The site engineer told me that the most important quality in engineering was double-checking every number.
Paragraph 3 (community benefit): An engineer helps the whole community, because safe roads, bridges and buildings let people travel, work and live without fear.
otherAnswers: Alternative profession, teacher: I would like to explain why I want to be a teacher. I chose this profession because my own teacher, Mr Yusuf, made even difficult lessons feel possible. Every day a teacher plans lessons, marks work and explains ideas patiently, sometimes several times over. It needs a teaching qualification and a great deal of patience. Mr Yusuf told me that the most important quality in teaching was believing every pupil can improve. A teacher helps the whole community, because every other profession begins with someone who was taught well.

Alternative profession, farmer: I would like to explain why I want to be a farmer. I chose this profession because my grandfather's small farm fed our whole extended family every season. Every day a farmer checks the soil, waters the crops and protects the animals from illness. It needs practical skill, patience and a good understanding of the weather. My grandfather told me that the most important quality in farming was noticing small changes early. A farmer helps the whole community, because without farmers nobody else would have food to eat.

writing.title: Writing 3: A Profession I Admire
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write a paragraph of six to eight sentences about a person you admire and the work they do. Begin with a topic sentence, use at least six words from this unit, and join your ideas with and, but and because. Underline the unit vocabulary you use.
writing.modelText: The person I admire most is my neighbour Amara, because her profession as a legal advisor helps people who cannot defend themselves. She studied for years and paid high tuition fees, but she never complains. Every day she reads long legal texts and writes careful observation notes for the court. When Mama Dina faced unfair penalties, Amara prepared her defence and explained the figures calmly. She listens to criticism with wisdom because she says every case teaches her something. I admire her because she uses her knowledge to protect other people, and one day I hope to do the same.

items: Sentence 1 (topic sentence): The person I admire most is my aunt Halima, because her profession as a nurse helps people at their most frightened moments.
Sentence 2 (joined with but): She studied for years and paid high tuition fees, but she never once complained about the cost.
Sentence 3: Every day she checks patients' figures, writes careful observation notes and explains treatments calmly.
Sentence 4 (specific example): When our neighbour faced a serious illness, Halima helped the family understand the diagnosis and stayed with them through a difficult decision.
Sentence 5 (joined with because): She listens to worried families with patience because she says every case teaches her something new.
Sentence 6 (closing, joined with and): I admire her because she uses her knowledge to protect other people, and one day I hope to do the same.
otherAnswers: Alternative person, a farmer: The person I admire most is my grandfather, because his profession as a farmer feeds our whole extended family every season. He works long hours and worries about the rain, but he never gives up on a difficult crop. Every day he checks the soil, waters carefully and protects the animals from illness. When the drought threatened our harvest last year, his careful planning meant we still had enough to share. He listens to advice from other farmers with real wisdom, because he says nobody learns everything alone. I admire him because his hard work quietly supports our whole family, and one day I hope to understand the land as well as he does.

Alternative person, a teacher: The person I admire most is my teacher, Mr Yusuf, because his profession shapes how an entire class of pupils sees the world. He marks work late into the evening, but he always returns it with useful comments. Every day he plans lessons, answers questions patiently and encourages pupils who find the work hard. When I struggled with fractions, he explained the idea three different ways until it finally made sense. He listens to every pupil's confusion with real wisdom, because he says confusion is simply the start of understanding. I admire him because his patience turns difficult ideas into knowledge, and one day I hope to explain things as clearly as he does.

writing.title: Writing 4: Information Report on a Profession
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write a short information report about one profession. Give it a heading, then write organised paragraphs that state at least five accurate facts about the job, the skills it requires and the tools or workplace it uses. Use precise unit vocabulary and check your spelling and punctuation carefully.
writing.modelText:
Pharmacist
A pharmacist prepares and sells medicines. In Hargeisa, most pharmacists work in a small shop next to a clinic or hospital.
The job needs a university degree in pharmacy and a licence from the government. A pharmacist must read a doctor's script carefully, check the figures on each dose and refuse to sell any medicine that is contaminated or out of date.
Pharmacists use scales, computers and locked cupboards to keep every item safe. Their wisdom and careful observation protect the whole community.

items: Heading: Electrician

Paragraph 1 (what the job involves): An electrician installs and repairs the wiring that brings power to homes, shops and schools. In many towns, electricians work alone or in small teams, moving between different job sites each day.

Paragraph 2 (skills and qualifications): The job needs a training certificate, a safety licence from the government and a steady, careful hand. An electrician must read wiring diagrams accurately, check every connection twice and refuse to leave a job that is not completely safe.

Paragraph 3 (tools, workplace and community link): Electricians use testers, insulated tools and protective gloves to keep every job safe. Their careful observation and technical wisdom protect whole buildings from fire and keep the community's lights on.
otherAnswers: Alternative profession, Midwife: heading 'Midwife', then organised facts. A midwife supports mothers through pregnancy and childbirth. In many communities, a midwife works in a clinic or travels directly to a family's home. The job needs medical training, a government licence and calm judgement under pressure. A midwife must monitor a mother's figures carefully and know exactly when to call for further help. Midwives use simple medical equipment and a great deal of experience, and their wisdom often makes the difference between a frightening birth and a safe one.

Alternative profession, Carpenter: heading 'Carpenter', then organised facts. A carpenter builds and repairs items made of wood, from furniture to roof frames. In many towns, a carpenter works from a small workshop or travels to a customer's house. The job needs practical training, careful measuring skills and safe use of sharp tools. A carpenter must check every measurement twice, because a small mistake can ruin an entire piece of furniture. Carpenters use saws, chisels and sandpaper, and their careful, patient observation turns raw wood into something a family will use for years.

writing.title: Writing 5: Reflect and Improve
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Choose one of your earlier pieces of writing from this unit. Revise three sentences to make them clearer, add two useful details, and then write a short paragraph explaining one improvement you made and why it makes the writing stronger.
writing.modelText:
In my job advertisement I wrote: We need someone good.
I changed it to: We need an efficient food inspector with a science certificate and two years of experience.
I also added the working hours and the salary, because a reader needs those figures before applying.
The new sentence is stronger because it names the profession with a compound noun and gives precise legal requirements, so the right person knows at once that the job is for them.

items: Revised sentence 1: 'She helps people' became 'Her profession as a nurse helps people at their most frightened moments', because naming the actual profession is clearer than a vague statement.
Revised sentence 2: 'She works hard' became 'She checks patients' figures, writes careful observation notes and explains treatments calmly', so the reader sees exactly what the work involves.
Revised sentence 3: 'People trust her' became 'When our neighbour faced a serious illness, Halima helped the family understand the diagnosis', which gives a real example instead of an empty claim.
Added detail 1: the specific example of the neighbour's illness, which makes the admiration feel earned rather than assumed.
Added detail 2: the phrase 'every case teaches her something new', which shows her attitude, not just her actions.

Reflection paragraph: My best improvement was replacing general statements with specific, precise details. This helps the reader understand exactly why I admire this profession instead of simply being told that I do.

writing.title: Writing 6: Courtroom News Report
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Imagine you are a journalist who watched Mama Dina's trial in 'Voices in the Courtroom'. Write a newspaper report of two organised paragraphs about what happened. Use reported speech to share what the different people said, for example: The judge said that the evidence had been incomplete, and include at least two compound nouns.
writing.modelText:
Luyanda Food Vendor Cleared After Trial
In a crowded Luyanda courtroom, Mama Dina, a local food vendor, was accused of selling contaminated cassava. The prosecution said that all vendors had to be inspected and that the penalties had to be applied equally. Mama Dina's lawyer told the court that the test results were incomplete and that the process had been unfair.

The prosecution said that every vendor had to follow the same food-safety rules and that the penalties needed to be applied fairly. Mama Dina's lawyer told the court that the laboratory results were incomplete and that the whole process had moved too quickly.

Paragraph 2 (verdict and reaction, two compound nouns): After careful observation of the test results, the judge said that the evidence had not proved the food was unsafe, and he withdrew the penalty. Outside the courthouse, Mama Dina told reporters that she was thankful for her legal advisor's hard work and would reopen her market stall the very next morning.

activities.title: Activities 1: Career Interview Role-Play
activities.instructionsAndItems: In this activity, one person plays the role of a worker and the other plays the role of a journalist. The journalist interviews the worker about their profession. Here is how to play. First, the worker chooses a profession, either one from this unit or any other job they know about. Second, the journalist prepares at least five questions to ask, such as: What does your job involve? What skills do you need? What is the most challenging part of your work? What advice would you give to a young person who wants to do this job? Third, the journalist asks the questions and listens carefully to the answers. Fourth, after the interview, the journalist reports what the worker said using reported speech. For example: She told me that her job involved reading legal documents. He said that the most challenging part was working long hours. Swap roles and play again with a different profession.
activities.answerSummary: Accept accurate responses supported by unit vocabulary, text evidence or a clear demonstration.

activities.title: Activities 2: Job Description Guessing Game
activities.instructionsAndItems: In this game, one person describes a job without saying the name of the profession. The listener must guess which job it is. Here is how to play. The speaker describes three things about the job: what the person does, where they work, and one tool or item they use. For example: This person writes scripts, speaks into a microphone, and works at a radio station. The listener guesses: A commentator! Try to play at least five rounds, using different jobs each time. After each round, the speaker should say one compound noun related to the job.

activities.title: Activities 3: Career Day Speech
activities.instructionsAndItems: Imagine your school is holding a Career Day and you have been asked to give a short talk about a profession. Prepare a one-to-two-minute speech. Your speech should include the name of the profession, what it involves, why it matters to the community, and why you think young people should consider it. Practise your speech before you deliver it. Speak clearly, make eye contact, and try to sound confident and enthusiastic. If you are working with a partner, ask them to listen and then report back to you what you said, using reported speech. This is a great way to practise both speaking and grammar at the same time.

grownUpGuide.label: Teacher & Parent Guide
grownUpGuide.intro: In this unit, your child works through "People and Work" on their own — new words, a grammar focus, and a set of longer readings. This guide shows you what they are working on so you can talk about it with them.

sections.title: 🧭 About this unit (please read first)
sections.body:
Your child is about 10-11 years old and works through this unit largely on their own — reading, practising and checking answers at their own pace. Your role is different from the early grades: you keep them company from outside the screen rather than leading each page.

The most useful things you can do are also the simplest: ask what the unit's texts are about, listen to them read a paragraph aloud, hear the new words used in sentences, and read their writing when they submit it. A few minutes of real conversation about the unit turns silent screen work into language they can actually use.

This guide tells you what the unit covers so you can ask good questions without working through the pages yourself.

sections.title: 💬 Using the AI Tutor with your child
sections.body:
At this age your child can use the AI Tutor on their own — it is worth sitting in occasionally to see how they use it, and showing them what it can do.

Suggest they ask it to quiz them on this unit's words: "Ask me questions about the word 'wisdom'."

Suggest they paste in a sentence of their own and ask whether it sounds natural, and how to say it better.

Encourage 'why' questions — why a comma goes there, why the text says it that way. Asking the tutor to explain, not just to check, is where the learning is.

sections.title: 🌟 Tips for supporting this unit
sections.body:
Short, regular sessions still beat one long one. A unit spread over several days sticks; a unit crammed in one sitting does not.

Talk about the reading away from the screen — over a meal, in the car. Retelling a text in their own words is one of the strongest checks of understanding there is.

Treat their writing as a draft to improve, not an answer to mark. Pick one thing to praise and one thing to sharpen, and stop there.

Praise precision and persistence, not just speed. At this stage careful, complete answers matter more than quick ones.

sections.title: How to Support This Unit, Step by Step
sections.body:
A simple shape for staying involved without taking over:

1. Before they start (2 min)
Skim this guide's word list and text titles so you know what to ask about later. You do not need to work through the pages yourself.

2. While they work
Let them work alone at their own pace. Be within reach for a word or an instruction they cannot crack, but resist doing the thinking for them.

3. Talk about the reading (5 min)
Ask them to tell you what "The People Who Keep a Community Running" was about in their own words, and what happened in "Voices in the Courtroom, part 1" — and what they thought of it.

4. Hear the words (5 min)
Pick a few words from the list below and ask for each one in a spoken sentence of their own. Saying a word out loud fixes it far better than reading it silently.

5. Check the grammar landed (3 min)
Ask them to explain "Compound Nouns: Closed, Hyphenated and Open Forms" to you as if you were the student. Teaching it back is the quickest way to find out whether it stuck.

6. Read their writing (5 min)
When the Writing section is submitted, read it together. Praise one specific thing, suggest one improvement, and leave it there.
